newsitem.title: USA: Black group threatened to "burn" St. Petersburg.
newsitem.headline: Black group threatened to "burn" St. Petersburg.

text.p: A second night of arson, rioting and gunfire in this Florida city this fall marked the latest in a long history of confrontations between a small but radical black group and city authorities.

Leaders of the National People's Democratic Uhuru Movement criticised the St. Petersburg police department after the first rioting in the city Oct. 24, following the shooting of a black motorist by a white police officer.
Members of the group publicly called for the execution of the two police officers involved in the shooting, the mayor of St. Petersburg and Police Chief Darrel Stephens.

Gunfire and arson were centred in the blocks around the Uhuru Movement's headquarters Wednesday, as the city was rocked by more rioting following a grand jury's decision not to indict the officer, James Knight.
Police said they tried to minimise unrest by confiscating tons of bottles, rocks and bricks the group had stockpiled before the grand jury verdict was expected.

"We've had threats, constant threats for the past two weeks, saying that if the report from the grand jury didn't meet with their satisfaction that the town was going to burn," Police Chief Darrel Stephens told reporters.

Police also arrested members of the group on outstanding traffic warrants Wednesday evening to keep them off the streets. But the strategy backfired, as Uhuru leader Omali Yeshitela was hit with pepper spray and tensions escalated.

Yeshitela, 55, has been a well known radical in St. Petersburg since 1964, when, as a reporter for the St. Petersburg Times, he was radicalized after a police beating because he was not carrying identification papers.
"He is very much a central figure. It's a cult of personality," said Raymond Arsenault, a professor of history at the University of South Florida in Tampa.

The beating inspired Yeshitela, then known as Joseph Waller, to lead a protest against a painting hung in City Hall that portrayed blacks in subservient roles. In 1966, after city officials refused to meet with him about the painting, he tore it down -- and did prison time as a result.

Following his release in 1968, he organised black sanitation workers in a strike that drew national attention and formed JOMO, the Junta of Militant Organisations, forerunner of the National People's Democratic Uhuru Movement.

In 1972, JOMO became the African People's Socialist Party, with chapters in about 20 cities. The group was modelled on the Black Panthers and advocated total separation of the races. In 1991 Yeshitela again changed the group's name, to the National People's Democratic Uhuru Movement.
Law enforcement estimates are that there are between 100 and 200 active Uhuru members in St. Petersburg, with about 2,000 people belonging to the group nationwide.
